Brian Chesky on why he stayed in Airbnb hosts' homes to figure out what to build:

"One of the most important pieces of advice I can probably give you is something that Paul Graham told me, and he said, 'It's better to have 100 people love you than a million people that just sort of like you.' Find 100 people and make them fall in love with your product, and you do that by doing things that don't scale."

"Sometimes the most important things you can do are the human moments. We went door to door signing people up. We went door to door living with people. When you bought an iPhone, Steve Jobs didn't come and stay in your house, but I did."

"We literally photographed people's homes. We helped them price it. We did everything. You see, the point is, as you design the perfect experience end to end, you do it by hand, and you recruit the community members one person at a time. They have a deep connection to you."

"The most important thing is to know what to build, and you don't know what to build if you're not with your customers, living with them, experiencing the world with them, especially in the offline world."

@bchesky on STATION Featuring, 2018

Ben Horowitz asked Mark Zuckerberg if 19 was too young to start a company:

"We were at this thing, the Herb Allen Sun Valley Conference... One of the things about this conference is they let you take your kids, but only until they're 20, and then they can't come anymore."

"And so my big one, Julia, is going, 'Oh, Dad, this is so great, but I can't come back because I'm going to be 20 next year. That's going to suck.' And I said, 'Well, you can come. Just become a real successful businessperson and then Herb will invite you back.' And she goes, 'That's ridiculous. I'm only 19 years old. I can't start a company.'"

"And we were sitting right next to Mark Zuckerberg. And I go, 'Mark, what do you think of that?' ... He goes, 'How old are you?' And she goes, '19.' He goes, 'Oh, bull crap, I was 19 when I started Facebook.'"

"Dads never get that on their teenagers. That was awesome. But the biggest thing about building a company, the biggest inhibitor to doing it is just believing that you can't. And so take it from Mark Zuckerberg. It is possible."

@bhorowitz at UC Berkeley, 2009

text:
Birth rate collapse in civilizations throughout history occurs whenever there is a long period of prosperity and no serious external threats. 

Rome had a very high birth rate during existential wars with Carthage and then very low after they had destroyed all external threats and had several generations of prosperity.

quoted_tweet.author: Homer Pavlos
quoted_tweet.text:
There was a demographic problem 2,200 years ago, and Polybius wrote exactly what caused it. Read carefully:

"In our times, Greece as a whole is experiencing a lack of children and, more generally, a decrease in population. Because of this, cities have become deserted and there is a lack of productivity, even though we do not suffer from constant wars or epidemics. So if someone advised that we send priests to the gods to ask them what we should say or do to become more numerous and better inhabit our cities, he would not seem foolish, since the cause is obvious and the solution lies in our own hands.

People have turned to arrogance, greed, and laziness, and they neither want to marry, nor, if they do marry, to raise their children. Instead, they have only one or two children with difficulty, just to leave them wealth and raise them in luxury.

This evil grew rapidly, and we did not notice. For when there are only one or two children, and one is lost to war and the other to illness, it is obvious that the cities will inevitably become deserted, just as a beehive weakens little by little, so too do cities that lack population become unable to survive."

Source: Histories, Polybius, 36 (ΛΣΤ)

The similarities after 2,200 years.

The demographic issue has been a problem several times throughout history, and none of those times was it due to the economy, but rather a result of prosperity, comfortable living, and laziness. My Greek grandparents had children even when they had nothing to eat, and the kids grew up barefoot, eating bread with olives and feta cheese. Money was never an obstacle.

Nowadays, people prefer partying, doing drugs, and living for today rather than having a purpose, building a family, and leaving a positive footprint in this world. They choose the easy life. It’s sad watching people who passionately want to have kids but can’t, compared to people who don’t want kids because it would take them out of their comfort zone, because a child would stop them from going to clubs, drinking, and partying like a meaningless person.

- Homer Pavlos

text: Prosperity, education, and urbanization are the stronger drivers. Global data show low-income countries averaging ~4.5 children per woman versus ~1.5 in high-income ones. Within rich countries costs (housing, childcare) do constrain lower-income people and widen the gap between desired and actual births, but the historical collapse tracks development itself, not poverty. Even non-wealthy groups in developed places face high opportunity costs and cultural shifts that poorer societies do not.
